html:
An empire that ruled much of northern India from the early 4th to the mid 6th century CE. It is often called India's golden age for its mathematics, science, Sanskrit literature and art, though historians argue over that label.

Its rise and fall:

  • Chandragupta I (from about 320) began the dynasty's era and strengthened it by marrying a princess of the Licchavi clan.
  • Samudragupta (about 335 to 375) campaigned across north India and as far south as the Pallava country. A poem carved on a pillar at Allahabad lists his victories.
  • Chandragupta II (about 375 to 415) conquered the Saka rulers of western India and gained ports on the Arabian Sea. The Chinese pilgrim Faxian travelled in his lands and found them peaceful. The rust-free Iron Pillar of Delhi probably comes from his reign.
  • Kumaragupta I (about 415 to 455) is credited with founding the monastery of Nalanda.
  • Skandagupta (about 455 to 467) drove back the Huns.

What came out of the period:

  • Aryabhata wrote his astronomy in 499, using a place-value number system.
  • Kalidasa, the greatest classical Sanskrit poet and playwright, probably lived in this time.
  • The first stone Hindu temples were built, and the Puranas took their final form.
  • Indians learned to make crystal sugar.
  • The Guptas issued fine gold coins.

From the late 5th century, attacks by the Alchon Huns and the breakaway of governors broke the empire apart. By about 550 the Gupta line had faded, and north India split into regional kingdoms until Harsha reunited much of it in the 7th century.
sum: An empire that ruled much of northern India from the early 4th to the mid 6th century CE. It is often called India's golden age for its mathematics, science, Sanskrit literature and art, though historians argue over that label.
